topic: El Nino: When the Ocean Shifts

sections.title: NORMAL PACIFIC
sections.narration: El Nino is a warming of the central and eastern tropical Pacific, with a matching change in the atmosphere. To understand it, first watch the normal ocean. Trade winds blow westward along the equator, pushing warm surface water toward Indonesia and Australia. Near South America, colder water rises from below. The warm pool helps air rise and clouds grow in the west. Wind, ocean, and rain work as one connected system.
sections.visual_thesis: The normal Pacific is an engine driven by wind and organized by temperature.
sections.visual_metaphor: A tilted reservoir of warm water with a cold fountain at the eastern edge.

sections.title: THE TILTED OCEAN
sections.narration: Now cut through the ocean along the equator. This drawing exaggerates depth so we can see its structure. Warm surface water sits above colder deep water. Their transition is called the thermocline. Normally, the wind piles warm water in the west, making that warm layer deeper. In the east, the thermocline lies closer to the surface. Upwelling brings colder, nutrient rich water upward, helping support marine life and important fisheries.
sections.visual_thesis: Trade winds tilt the ocean's hidden thermal boundary.
sections.visual_metaphor: A sloping invisible floor separates a warm upper layer from a cold reservoir.

sections.title: THE WIND RELAXES
sections.narration: During El Nino, the trade winds weaken. Some bursts of wind can even blow eastward. Warm water spreads toward the central and eastern Pacific. The thermocline rises in the west and deepens in the east, becoming less tilted. Upwelling becomes less effective at cooling the eastern surface. The warmer ocean changes rising air and wind, which can reinforce the original warming. This is a feedback between the ocean and atmosphere.
sections.visual_thesis: El Nino is a coupled shift: weaker winds let warm water move, and warm water weakens the winds further.
sections.visual_metaphor: A tilted basin levels out and its warm layer rolls toward the opposite shore.

sections.title: RAIN FOLLOWS THE HEAT
sections.narration: The warmest water is a source of heat and moisture for the air above it. Rising moist air helps clouds and rain develop. Normally, strong tropical rainfall is concentrated near the western warm pool. As El Nino develops, the center of convection moves toward the central and eastern Pacific. Rainfall can increase there, while Indonesia and parts of Australia face greater drought risk. The rain belt has moved because the ocean changed.
sections.visual_thesis: Rainfall is carried by the warm-water center, not pinned to a continent.
sections.visual_metaphor: A moving cloud crown follows the heat like a spotlight crossing the ocean.

sections.title: ONE OCEAN, MANY RESPONSES
sections.narration: The influence reaches beyond the tropical Pacific. Moving the region of rising air changes large scale atmospheric circulation and distant storm tracks. Coastal Peru may experience heavier rainfall, while parts of Indonesia and Australia become drier. Other regions respond through atmospheric teleconnections. These are shifts in probability, not promises. Impacts depend on the season, the strength of the event, and other climate patterns.
sections.visual_thesis: A basin-scale ocean anomaly sends atmospheric consequences across the globe.
sections.visual_metaphor: One glowing region on a globe tugs several distant weather threads.

sections.title: THE ENSO SEESAW
sections.narration: El Nino is the warm phase of ENSO, the El Nino Southern Oscillation. La Nina is its cool phase. Stronger trade winds push warm water farther west, while colder water reaches the eastern surface more effectively. Between them lies a neutral state. These phases return irregularly, often over two to seven years, rather than on a fixed schedule. The lesson is simple: wind moves ocean heat, and ocean heat reorganizes weather.
sections.visual_thesis: ENSO is an ocean-atmosphere seesaw, not a single hot or cold day.
sections.visual_metaphor: Two opposing lanes show the same Pacific basin switching its circulation state.
